beats.intro: Chapter one, lesson four. The metabolic classification. [[plate]]Picture a plate of beans and an egg. Your body breaks the protein into amino acids, and uses some of them as fuel. [[card]]Here is our amino acid card, and today the last tab lights up: metabolic. [[tab]]This tab asks one question. The nitrogen is taken off first, and what is left is the carbon skeleton. When the body breaks an amino acid down, what does that skeleton become? Glucose, ketone bodies, or both?
beats.fork: [[fork]]Think of a road that forks in two. [[glc]]One branch ends at glucose. The slide calls it carbohydrate, and glucose is the carbohydrate your blood carries. An amino acid whose skeleton goes down this branch is called glucogenic, because it can be made into glucose. [[ket]]The other branch ends at ketone bodies, a fuel the liver makes from small carbon pieces. An amino acid on this branch is called ketogenic. [[both]]And some amino acids send part of the skeleton down each branch. Those are the mixed ones: both glucogenic and ketogenic. [[three]]So there are three classes. Ketogenic, mixed, and glucogenic.
beats.keto: [[ll]]Start with the smallest group. Only two amino acids are purely ketogenic: leucine and lysine. The slide's mnemonic is two L's. Leucine, lysine. [[tag]]Their skeletons give ketone bodies only. They never become glucose. [[link]]Notice that both are essential amino acids, so they come from the diet. Leucine you met as a branched-chain amino acid, and lysine as a basic one.
beats.q1: Quick check. Which two amino acids are purely ketogenic?
beats.mixed: [[fit]]Next, the mixed group. Five amino acids give both glucose and ketone bodies. The mnemonic is fit, with three T's. [[f]]The first letter is phenylalanine. [[i]]The I is isoleucine. [[t1]]The first T is tyrosine. [[t2]]The second T is tryptophan. [[t3]]And the last T is threonine. [[ring]]See the rings? Phenylalanine and tyrosine are the aromatic pair, and tryptophan has its indole ring. [[split]]For each of these five, the skeleton splits. Part goes to glucose, and part goes to ketone bodies.
beats.gluco: [[rest]]Everything else is glucogenic only. That is the remaining thirteen. [[names]]Alanine, arginine, asparagine, aspartic acid, glutamic acid, glutamine, glycine, cysteine, histidine, methionine, proline, serine, and valine. [[tip]]There is no mnemonic for these, and you do not need one. If it is not leucine, not lysine, and not in fit with three T's, it is glucogenic. Learn the short lists, and the long list is simply everything else. [[trio]]One trap. The three branched-chain amino acids are cousins, but they take three different roads. Valine is glucogenic, isoleucine is mixed, and leucine is ketogenic.
beats.count: [[count]]Let's check that the books balance. Two ketogenic, five mixed, thirteen glucogenic. [[sum]]Two plus five is seven, and seven plus thirteen is twenty. All twenty standard amino acids, each filed once. [[ten]]So eighteen of the twenty can make glucose: the thirteen, plus the five mixed. And seven of the twenty can make ketone bodies: the two, plus the five mixed.
beats.q2: Quick check. How many amino acids can make glucose? Count the glucogenic ones and the mixed ones.
beats.fast: [[meal]]Why does this matter? [[fast]]Think of a long fast, many hours without food. Blood glucose has to stay up, and the liver can make new glucose from glucogenic skeletons. That is what a glucogenic amino acid is good for. [[ketone]]If the fast goes on, the liver also makes ketone bodies, a fuel that many tissues, the brain among them, can burn. Ketogenic amino acids feed that fuel, but they cannot add to glucose. [[light]]This is only the outline. How these pathways work comes later, in a course on metabolism.
beats.recap: [[card2]]Now the whole chapter on one card. We take one amino acid, lysine, and fill all four tabs. [[s]]Structural. By its side chain, lysine is aliphatic, and that side chain ends in an amino group, so it is one of the basic aliphatic amino acids. [[c]]Chemical. It has two amino groups and one carboxyl group, so it is basic, with a positive charge. [[n]]Nutritional. The body cannot make it, so lysine is essential, and must come from the diet. [[m]]Metabolic. Its skeleton gives ketone bodies only, so it is ketogenic. [[all]]One amino acid, four tabs: aliphatic basic, basic, essential, ketogenic. [[tyr]]Try tyrosine yourself. Aromatic, neutral, non-essential, and mixed.
beats.wrap: [[wrap]]So we classify by the side chain, by the charge, by the diet, and by the fate of the skeleton. Four ways of looking at the same twenty amino acids. Remember the three metabolic lists. Two L's are ketogenic. Fit with three T's is mixed. The other thirteen are glucogenic. [[next]]Next chapter turns to what these amino acids build: proteins.
